tagline: Sand pine, clear springs and a river town reached by steamboat
intro: The Florida Black Bear Scenic Byway follows a 60-mile stretch of SR 40 from Silver Springs to Interstate 95, with additional loops and spurs. Its corridor takes in the Ocala National Forest and the Big Scrub, where sand pine grows on ancient dunes. The Federal Highway Administration describes long, undisturbed stretches of natural Florida along this National Scenic Byway. Florida’s scenic-highway program highlights its springs, trails and waterways. The region has Florida’s highest density of black bears, which the state byway program says are often close to the road.

The forest received federal designation from President Theodore Roosevelt in 1908. A century later, the road corridor gained its own recognition: Florida designated the byway on April 9, 2008, followed by national designation in 2009. Ocala is the oldest national forest east of the Mississippi River.

For a forest excursion, Salt Springs lies on SR 19 within the Ocala National Forest. The SR 40 backbone begins at Silver Springs, then passes Lynne on the forest’s western edge. Farther east, Astor straddles SR 40 on the west bank of the St. Johns River. Beyond the river, Barberville marks the junction with U.S. 17 before the byway’s eastern end at I-95.

moments.title: Salt Springs
moments.text: At Salt Springs, clear water stays at 72°F year round, and the spring feeds Lake George. Bass, turtles and blue crabs share the springs. The community lies within the Ocala National Forest, near Lake George, with SR 19 among its main roads. The springs are the focus of a recreation and camping area; neighboring Lake Kerr provides another setting for water sports.

moments.title: Silver Springs
moments.text: Glass-bottom boats made the springs visible beneath the visitor’s feet. Hullam Jones and Phillip Morell developed glass-bottom boats and rowboats in the late 1870s, when tourists were reaching the springs by steamboat. The attraction later became a film location, including for several Tarzan movies. Florida bought the main attraction in 1993 while private management continued. In 2013, it combined Silver Springs with the adjacent Silver River State Park. Glass-bottom boats remain based at the former theme-park site. The park also contains sandhill forests and wetlands, with the spring-fed Silver River flowing into the Ocklawaha.
moments.notice: Glass-bottom boats reveal the river’s springs and wildlife.

moments.title: Astor
moments.text: Astor began as William Backhouse Astor Jr.’s town-building venture under another name: Manhattan. He bought more than 12,000 acres in 1874, and settlers arrived by steamboat. Astor supplied a church, schoolhouse and cemetery, then added a railroad toward Eustis and Leesburg. Manhattan never caught on; after his death in 1892 the town officially became Astor. The first Astor Bridge followed in 1926. By 1928, the hotel had burned and the railroad was abandoned, leaving the town without telephone or telegraph service for decades. The community now straddles SR 40 beside the St. Johns, between Lake George and Lake Dexter.
